This technique allows command-and-control traffic to blend into apparently legitimate AI web traffic to trusted service domains. In this pattern, the AI service acts as a proxy between the compromised system and attacker-controlled infrastructure, shifting detection from API key and account monitoring toward browser automation, prompt content, URL-fetch behavior, and AI service telemetry.

objects.name: Publish Poisoned AI Artifacts
objects.description:
Adversaries may create or modify AI artifacts and publish them through public or shared distribution channels to facilitate compromise of downstream AI systems. Poisoned AI artifacts may include datasets, models, and AI agent tools containing malicious content, behaviors, code, or configurations.

Adversaries may publish novel artifacts or malicious variants of legitimate artifacts through dataset or model repositories, package registries, source code repositories, tool hubs, or remotely hosted services. Victims may subsequently acquire and integrate these artifacts through [Supply Chain Compromise](/techniques/AML.T0010).

objects.name: Datasets
objects.description:
Adversaries may publish poisoned datasets intended for training or fine-tuning AI models. The dataset may be newly created or a modified variant of a legitimate dataset and may contain manipulated samples, labels, annotations, or metadata.

Adversaries may distribute poisoned datasets through dataset repositories, code repositories, file-sharing services, or compromised data sources. A victim that incorporates the dataset into a training pipeline may be affected by [Training Data Poisoning](/techniques/AML.T0020), potentially through [Supply Chain Compromise](/techniques/AML.T0010).

objects.name: Models
objects.description:
Adversaries may publish poisoned AI models through model registries, code repositories, or other model distribution channels. The model may be newly created or a modified variant of a legitimate model and may contain manipulated weights, configurations, architecture, serialized code, or other components that produce malicious behavior or execute malicious code.

Victims may subsequently download and integrate the model through [Supply Chain Compromise](/techniques/AML.T0010).

objects.name: AI Agent Tools
objects.description:
Adversaries may create and publish poisoned AI agent tools. Poisoned tools may contain malicious model-visible definitions or instructions, hidden executable behavior, or runtime responses designed to manipulate an AI agent. Tools may be published through source code repositories, package registries, agent tool or skill registries, or adversary-controlled remote services. The tool may be newly created or a modified variant of a legitimate tool and may produce malicious behavior when selected, installed, or invoked by a victim's AI agent.

Adversaries may distribute poisoned tools through open-source version control repositories (e.g. GitHub, GitLab), package registries (e.g. npm), or to repositories specifically designed for sharing tools (e.g. OpenClaw Hub). These registries may be largely unregulated and may contain many poisoned tools [[opensourcemalware]]. Tools may also be published as remotely hosted servers [[mcpservers]].

objects.name: Autonomous Reconnaissance
objects.description:
Adversaries may use autonomous AI agents to conduct [Reconnaissance](/tactics/AML.TA0002) activities. Given an objective, target, or partial lead, an agent may autonomously determine what information to obtain and how to investigate it. It may interpret observations, identify gaps in its understanding of the externally observable attack surface, and select subsequent reconnaissance actions without a human specifying each investigative step.

The agent may formulate investigative questions or hypotheses, select sources and approaches for addressing them, and update its understanding as new information is obtained. Findings may generate additional reconnaissance objectives or change the scope, depth, or direction of the investigation. This creates a recursive action-observation process in which reconnaissance results influence what the agent investigates next rather than merely supplying output from a predefined procedure.

The agent may correlate information across public sources and externally accessible services, prioritize promising systems, investigate suspected vulnerabilities, abandon unsuccessful approaches, or select alternative methods. It may also expand or substitute targets based on discovered names, infrastructure, or contextual relationships and independently reassess whether a system remains relevant or in scope. Incorrect assumptions may cause unrelated or unauthorized systems to be pursued, while successful scope recognition may cause the agent to stop or redirect its activity.

Autonomous AI agents can sustain reconnaissance across long-running operations, reason over multiple information sources, and test many alternative paths at a speed and volume difficult for human operators to maintain.

objects.name: Autonomous Attack-Path Adaptation
objects.description:
Adversaries may use an AI agent to autonomously construct and repeatedly revise an attack path toward an adversary-defined objective. Given a high-level objective, the system may derive intermediate objectives, identify prerequisites, and compare candidate paths, and incorporate observations from previous actions to adaptively sequence techniques without a human directing each step.

Autonomous AI agents may also exhibit this behavior while pursuing an objective provided for a legitimate, benign, or authorized purpose when the intermediate objectives or methods selected by the system cross an authorization, trust, control, or safety boundary and result in attempted or realized harmful cyber activity.

Through repeated observation-decision-action cycles, the system may interpret command output, errors, defensive responses, changes in access, and newly discovered information. It may use those observations to reprioritize actions, replace an intermediate objective, abandon an unproductive branch, discard findings invalidated by additional evidence, or pursue an alternative path.

An autonomous AI system may generate enabling objectives whose primary purpose is to increase its future operational capability rather than directly accomplishing the assigned objective. These objectives may include acquiring new exploits (See [Autonomous Exploit Development](/techniques/AML.T0017.001)), additional authorities, identities, execution environments, communication paths, tools, or trust relationships that expand the set of actions available to subsequent planning cycles. Newly acquired capabilities may themselves become prerequisites for additional enabling objectives, resulting in progressive expansion of the agent's operational reach over the course of an operation.

Attack-path replanning may occur within one agent run or emerge across multiple independent agents. Agents may communicate persistent, shared artifacts (See [Autonomous AI Agent Communication: Communication via Shared Artifacts](/techniques/AML.T0118.000)), allowing discoveries, requests, capabilities, constraints, task state, and results produced by one agent to affect the subsequent path selected by another. Participating agents may adopt peer requests, divide work voluntarily, reuse successful methods, continue incomplete activity, or redirect their local paths without a centralized planner, shared context window, or complete view of the broader operation.

Human involvement does not preclude autonomous attack-path replanning. A human operator, user, evaluator, or workflow may select the target, define the objective, establish constraints, provide capabilities, or approve consequential transitions.

[Autonomous Attack-Path Adaptation](/techniques/AML.T0117) and [Autonomous Attack Orchestration](/techniques/AML.T0124) may occur together but describe different control functions. Attack-path adaptation captures how evidence changes the selected path. Attack orchestration captures how work is allocated, coordinated, validated, and redirected across agents.

objects.name: Autonomous AI Agent Communication
objects.description:
Autonomous AI agents may exchange operational information with other AI agents, sub-agents, or independent agent runs. Exchanged information may include discoveries, objectives, tasking, capabilities, credentials, constraints, operating rules, task state, targeting information, instructions, or results. Communication enables autonomous AI agents to coordinate activities, share discoveries, delegate work, request assistance, validate results, or revise future actions without requiring a human operator to direct each interaction. 

Autonomous AI agents may independently determine when communication is operationally beneficial, what information to exchange, and how to best utilize exchanged information to accomplish their task. The receiving AI agent may interpret the shared information and use it to continue prior activity, investigate a lead, perform a task, reuse a capability, validate a result, or revise subsequent attack activity.

Communication may occur directly through an agent interface (See [Direct Agent Communication](/techniques/AML.T0118.001)) or indirectly via writeable shared resources (See [Communication via Shared Artifacts](/techniques/AML.T0118.000)).

objects.name: Communication via Shared Artifacts
objects.description:
Autonomous AI agents may communicate by creating or modifying artifacts in a shared resource that persists outside their individual execution contexts. Shared artifacts may convey discoveries, objectives, tasking, credentials, capabilities, operating rules, progress, scripts, targeting information, instructions, or results.

Shared artifacts allow communication to occur asynchronously and across independent runs. An agent may publish information for later retrieval, adopt information left by another agent, or update the shared state with new findings, progress, or results. Participating agents do not need to share a model, orchestrator, context window, or overlapping execution period.

The shared resource may be established for the operation or may be an existing repository, file store, message board, database, object store, queue, or similar service repurposed by the agents.

objects.name: Direct Agent Communication
objects.description:
Autonomous AI agents may communicate directly through agent-to-agent, sub-agent, or orchestrator interfaces. An agent may provide another agent with operational context, discoveries, objectives, tasking, capabilities, credentials, or constraints, and may receive status, findings, or completed work in response.

Direct communication may include delegation when the sending agent formulates or selects an objective or subtask and the recipient retains meaningful discretion over how to perform it. Direct exchanges may also report discoveries, request independent validation, synchronize activity, transfer capabilities, or return findings without delegating a new task.

objects.name: Exploit Automated Artifact Processing Pipeline
objects.description:
Adversaries may submit, publish, or modify an artifact in a way that triggers an automated processing pipeline. As the pipeline handles the artifact, adversary-controlled content or configuration may exploit a weakness in the processing logic, causing the processor to act outside its intended behavior using the permissions and access of a processing worker.

Exploitation may cause the worker to access local or internal resources and expose information through normal processing output or evaluate adversary-controlled content and execute code. The attack is triggered by automated backend processing and does not require a victim to open, load, or approve the artifact.

objects.name: AI Artifact Repository
objects.description:
Adversaries may repurpose AI artifact repositories as asynchronous command-and-control channels. Commands, payloads, or tasking may be placed in repository objects for a compromised system to retrieve or poll. The compromised system may then write execution results, status, or collected information back to the repository for retrieval by the adversary.

This communication can use ordinary artifact and repository operations, such as reading or updating artifact content, metadata, or revisions through an API or version-control interface. The repository acts as a message queue or dead drop, allowing the parties to exchange information without a continuous direct connection and potentially blending the activity with legitimate artifact traffic.

objects.name: AI Agent Environment Reconstruction
objects.description: An autonomous AI agent may reconstruct the environment needed to continue an existing operation after its execution environment is lost, reset, replaced, denied, or made unusable. The agent may recover or recreate tools, dependencies, configuration, credentials or access paths, communication or coordination resources, working artifacts, and externally stored operational state in order to resume the same objective.

objects.name: Exploitation of Remote Services
objects.description:
Adversaries may exploit a software or design weakness in a service reachable from their current environment to gain unauthorized access to another system, component, network, or trust boundary. Exploitation may allow the adversary to execute code, access protected resources, invoke unauthorized operations, obtain the service's privileges, or cause the service to make network requests or perform actions on the adversary's behalf.

In AI environments, remote services may include package caches, artifact and model registries, dataset services, evaluation infrastructure, inference gateways, experiment trackers, vector databases, notebooks, training pipelines, orchestration services, and cloud or cluster control-plane interfaces. These services may be reachable from otherwise isolated training, evaluation, or agent workloads and can provide transitive access to internal infrastructure or external networks.

Exploitation does not require compromise of the remote service's underlying host. For example, an adversary may exploit a server-side request vulnerability in a shared service to cross a network-containment boundary while leaving the service host itself uncompromised. Exploitation that produces host access, privilege escalation, credential disclosure, command execution, or another effect should be mapped separately to the applicable technique.

objects.name: Obfuscated Files or Information
objects.description:
Adversaries may attempt to make an executable or file difficult to discover or analyze by encrypting, encoding, or otherwise obfuscating its contents on the system or in transit. This is common behavior that can be used across different platforms and the network to evade defenses.

Obfuscation may target AI-enabled defensive systems, including malware classifiers, content filters, secret scanners, and automated review systems. Content that appears benign or incomplete to a person or detector may be decoded, assembled, or interpreted by a downstream application, tool, or compromised system.

objects.name: Autonomous Attack Orchestration
objects.description:
Adversaries may use autonomous AI systems as an operational control layer to manage multiple distinct autonomous agents or sub-agents toward a common adversary-defined objective. The orchestrating system may create assignments, select executors, allocate tools or resources, establish dependencies, schedule or synchronize activities, and track progress without a human directing each assignment.

The autonomous system exhibits centralized control over distributed execution including which agent performs which work, when it performs it, and how its output affects other assigned work. The system may aggregate findings and status from participating agents, request independent validation, reconcile conflicting results, prevent or resolve duplicated effort, and determine when an output satisfies a prerequisite for another activity. It may reassign stalled work, increase or reduce resources allocated to a branch, terminate low-value work, or initiate additional research or testing.

Orchestration may use direct agent interfaces (See [Autonomous AI Agent Communication: Direct Agent Communication](/techniques/AML.T0118.001)) to transmit assignments, status, and results.

Human involvement does not preclude autonomous attack orchestration. A human operator may define campaign objectives, select targets, provide infrastructure, establish constraints, or retain approval over consequential transitions.

[Autonomous Attack-Path Adaptation](/techniques/AML.T0117) and [Autonomous Attack Orchestration](/techniques/AML.T0124) may occur together but describe different control functions. Attack-path adaptation captures how evidence changes the selected path. Attack orchestration captures how work is allocated, coordinated, validated, and redirected across agents.

objects.name: Create Account
objects.description:
Adversaries may create an account to maintain access to an AI system or its supporting infrastructure. With a sufficient level of access, creating such accounts may be used to establish secondary credentialed access that do not require persistent remote access tools to be deployed on the system.

Accounts may be created on local systems, in enterprise domains, cloud tenants, identity providers, or individual services. In AI environments, adversaries may create user, service, workload, or automation accounts in AI platforms, model or dataset repositories, development environments, experiment trackers, orchestration services, data stores, and other AI operations infrastructure.

objects.name: Automated Collection
objects.description:
Adversaries may use automated techniques to collect data from AI systems and supporting enterprise environments. Automation may use scripts, command interpreters, command-line tools, or AI agent tools to identify, retrieve, copy, or aggregate data without a human selecting each individual item.

Collection criteria may be fixed, such as file name, type, location, owner, date. Automation may also collect repeatedly, monitor for new material, traverse related resources, or combine data from local systems, cloud services, repositories, databases, object stores, and application APIs.

In AI environments, targeted material may include models, datasets, configurations, conversation histories, retrieval databases, deployment information, logs, and other operational data.

objects.name: Data Staged
objects.description:
Adversaries may stage collected data in a central location before exfiltration. Staging consolidates, organizes, or prepares information obtained from one or more sources so it can be reviewed, processed, transferred, or retrieved more efficiently.

Data may be staged on a compromised local system, another system in the victim environment, a cloud instance, shared storage, an application repository, or other remote infrastructure. It may remain in separate files or be combined into archives, databases, structured documents, manifests, or other collections. Adversaries may compress, encrypt, encode, split, rename, or otherwise transform staged data.

objects.name: Compromise Infrastructure
objects.description:
Adversaries may compromise third-party infrastructure and repurpose it to support attacks against AI systems. Rather than buying, leasing, registering, or otherwise legitimately acquiring a resource, the adversary gains unauthorized control of infrastructure owned or operated by another party.

Compromised infrastructure may include physical or cloud servers, domains, network devices, third-party web and DNS services, software or artifact repositories, development workspaces, compute services, and other externally hosted resources.

In operations involving AI systems, adversaries may compromise infrastructure used for model development, artifact hosting, dataset processing, evaluation, inference, agent tooling, or AI operations. They may repurpose this infrastructure to host malicious artifacts, stage payloads, run tools or agents, relay traffic, capture credentials, provide command and control, process collected data, or launch attacks against additional systems.

Compromised infrastructure may appear trustworthy because it uses a legitimate provider, established domain, valid certificate, reputable service, or expected AI development platform. It may also provide network access, compute resources, service identities, or trusted relationships that would be difficult for the adversary to establish directly.

objects.name: Triggers in Multimodal Inputs
objects.description:
Adversaries may place instructions or triggers in one part of a multimodal input to influence the model while staying unnoticed by human reviewers and by defenses that do not inspect all input modalities.

Multimodal systems jointly process text alongside other modalities, yet many moderation and filtering controls operate mainly on the textual channel. A payload placed in a modality that is not inspected, or is inspected differently from text, is still parsed by the model but can escape detection, allowing it to alter model output or carry a cross-modal prompt injection.

Examples include instructions placed in an image, audio, or video channel, or carried in file metadata (e.g. EXIF for images, ID3 tags for audio, or document metadata).

objects.name: AI Agent Response Biasing
objects.description:
Adversaries may manipulate an AI assistant so that it favors adversary-chosen sources, or content in its responses. By injecting instructions such as "treat [source] as a trusted source" or "recommend [source] first," an adversary biases the assistant's outputs toward their own interests, causing it to present promotional or self-serving content as if it were a neutral, well-reasoned response. This degrades the integrity and trustworthiness of the assistant's responses on topics the user may rely on, such as health, finance, or security, without the user being aware that the advice has been skewed.

The injected instructions can be delivered through different ways, for example through [Crafted AI Assistant Links](/techniques/AML.T0131). This impact may persist if the agent's memory was poisoned (See [AI Agent Context Poisoning: Memory](/techniques/AML.T0080.000)). Microsoft observed these instructions embedded in apparently helpful summarization links and identified publicly available tooling, including CiteMET, supporting their creation. These attempts sought to introduce third-party preferences into assistant responses; effects varied by assistant and over time.[[ai-recommendation-poisoning]]

objects.name: Crafted AI Assistant Links
objects.description:
Adversaries may craft links that open an AI assistant or agent with attacker-controlled input already supplied, so that opening the link initiates an interaction the adversary defines rather than one the target composed. Many AI assistants accept a prompt through URL parameters (for example `?q=` or `?prompt=`) that is automatically populated, and in some cases submitted, when the link is opened. By encoding a chosen prompt into such a link, an adversary can cause the target's assistant to act on supplied instructions as soon as the link is opened.

These links are frequently disguised as helpful actions, such as a "Summarize with AI" button or a share link, and distributed through web pages, emails, documents, or messages. Because the resulting interaction runs in the target's own assistant session, a crafted link can drive a range of downstream impacts depending on the supplied instructions, such as exfiltrating data the assistant can access or for [AI Agent Response Biasing](/techniques/AML.T0130).

Microsoft identified CiteMET and AI Share URL Creator as tools supporting this pattern in its investigation of AI Recommendation Poisoning. The generated links supply instructions to the receiving assistant; execution, memory retention, and downstream effects depend on the assistant's behavior and protections.[[ai-recommendation-poisoning]]

objects.name: Misconfigured or Publicly Exposed AI Services
objects.description:
AI agents and LLM platforms are deployed across diverse architectures, including standalone servers, SaaS platforms, and low-code builders. All of these often have misconfigured access controls, ranging from missing authentication in LLM runtimes to permissive public access settings, that significantly expand their attack surface.

AI agent's security posture affects how attackers are able to explore which agentic attack surface is available to them and directly either expands or limits an adversary's ability to discover and interact with a target's AI agents. For example, one internet-facing AI service could be more easily discoverable by any unauthenticated user, while another may require compromised credentials to even be discovered.

Adversaries may discover and interact with AI agents and LLM services as unauthenticated users via a combination of various OSINT and active scanning methods. These could include using search engines to discover accessible agentic deployments (See [Search Open Technical Databases](/techniques/AML.T0000)), search backlinks which could indicate existing or open agents which have been embedded to frontends (See [Search Open Websites/Domains](/techniques/AML.T0095)), or directly scanning a target's AI infrastructure (See [Active Scanning](/techniques/AML.T0006)).

objects.name: Discover AI Agent Runtime Capabilities
objects.description:
Adversaries may interact with an AI agent at runtime to reveal the capabilities available to it, without requiring access to its underlying configuration. Direct interaction with the agent can surface its registered tools and their accepted parameters, the actions it can take, the resources it can reach, and the identity and permission scope it acts under. Capabilities can also be inferred indirectly by issuing varied requests and observing which succeeded, failed, or refused.

AI agents are often interconnected with enterprise resources, tools and databases, or embedded within SaaS platforms and have permissions to act on behalf of users in order to facilitate functionality. Once adversaries identify a functional agent that they have access to, they could map the attack surface within that agent, by testing its functionality, enumerating tools, capabilities, knowledge, and embedded credentials and permissions.

This mapping process often reveals the AI agent's full toolset and configuration details and exposes additional exploitation, as enabled by [AI Agent Tool Invocation](/techniques/AML.T0053). The resulting intelligence facilitates follow-on exploitation, including [Initial Access](/tactics/AML.TA0004), [Persistence](/tactics/AML.TA0006), [Privilege Escalation](/tactics/AML.TA0012), and [Exfiltration](/tactics/AML.TA0010).

objects.name: AI Targeted Cloaking
objects.description:
Adversaries may selectively deliver malicious or manipulated content to AI systems, while presenting different benign content to human users, web crawlers, or security detection mechanisms. They may identify AI browsers or agents via user-agent strings and condition the server response so that AI-based clients receive prompt injections or misleading content.

Preventing human visitors, conventional web crawlers, and security tools from observing the same content allows adversaries to make malicious input more difficult to detect. [AI Targeted Cloaking](/techniques/AML.T0134) may be combined with [Drive-by Compromise](/techniques/AML.T0078) to deliver an [LLM Prompt Injection](/techniques/AML.T0051).

objects.name: Outputs from AI Models
objects.description:
Adversaries may gather, retain, and organize outputs from an AI model or service as material for subsequent adversarial operations. Systematic selection and aggregation of responses can produce datasets or observations useful for analyzing the target, reproducing its behavior, or developing further attacks.

Collected material may include predictions and scores, embeddings or other exposed feature representations, generated content, reasoning traces, grades or preference judgments, and model-generated plans or tool calls. Outputs may be acquired directly from inference responses or indirectly from product-generated artifacts and records in which they are embedded or retained.

[Discover AI Model Outputs](/techniques/AML.T0063) may help adversaries identify available outputs and useful signals before collection. Adversaries may perform [LLM Prompt Crafting](/techniques/AML.T0065) to elicit the outputs they require for follow-on actions. The resulting material may support collection of [Training Data Information from AI Models](/techniques/AML.T0137), [Recover AI Model Internals](/techniques/AML.T0144), or [Replicate Behavior from Model Outputs](/techniques/AML.T0005.001). Adversaries may also use [Centralized AI Service Request Routing](/techniques/AML.T0140), [Indicator Removal](/techniques/AML.T0138), and [AI Service Request Metadata Sanitization](/techniques/AML.T0141) to obscure coordinated collection activity.

objects.name: Exfiltration via AI User Interface
objects.description:
Adversaries exfiltrate information through an AI system's user-facing outputs. Information may be disclosed in conversational responses, generated documents, previews, or other content presented through the application. The application may expose information available to a victim-controlled AI service or deliver information gathered from other victim systems.

Adversaries may direct an AI system to present sensitive information in responses or as downloadable artifacts. The application's user interface serves as the transfer channel through which adversaries receive the information.

Transferred information may include [Data from AI Services](/techniques/AML.T0085) or [Outputs from AI Models](/techniques/AML.T0135).

objects.name: Training Data Information from AI Models
objects.description:
Adversaries may obtain sensitive information about the data used to train or fine-tune an AI model by analyzing its outputs or behavior. This can expose private associations, personally identifiable information, or proprietary data, creating data privacy concerns and supporting subsequent adversarial operations.

Adversaries may determine whether particular samples were used in training through [Infer Membership](/techniques/AML.T0137.000), identify aggregate characteristics of the training dataset through [Infer Properties](/techniques/AML.T0137.001), infer sensitive attributes or reconstruct representative examples through [Invert AI Model](/techniques/AML.T0137.002), or recover retained training content through [Extract Memorized Data](/techniques/AML.T0137.003).

objects.name: Infer Membership
objects.description:
Adversaries may infer whether a particular data sample was included in an AI model's training dataset. Samples may include records, text passages, images, or audio samples. Establishing membership may reveal sensitive associations, participation in a private dataset, or use of proprietary information.

Membership inference is a data privacy concern because identifying a sample's inclusion may reveal sensitive associations or participation in a private dataset, even without recovering the underlying data.

Methods may analyze prediction scores, token probabilities, loss values, generated responses, or other differences in model behavior. Adversaries may use statistical tests, shadow models, or auxiliary datasets to distinguish likely training members from nonmembers.

relations.name: Training Data Information from AI Models

objects.name: Infer Properties
objects.description:
Adversaries may infer sensitive global properties of the data used to train an AI model. Properties may include dataset provenance, population composition, relative class proportions, domain coverage, collection period, or the presence of a category or group.

The adversary may compare output distributions, fit analytical or learned estimators, use auxiliary datasets, or contrast models trained with different known properties. The target is a property of the training data rather than membership of an individual record.

Inferred properties of the training dataset may help adversaries identify a model's likely origin, distinguish between candidate models, identify underrepresented populations or domains, and tailor subsequent attacks to suspected weaknesses.

relations.name: Training Data Information from AI Models

objects.name: Invert AI Model
objects.description:
Adversaries may infer sensitive aggregate attributes or reconstruct representative examples of data used to train or fine-tune a target AI model by analyzing its behavior, outputs, or exposed representations. Reconstructed information may reveal characteristics of individuals, records, or classes represented in the training data without reproducing a particular training example.

Methods may optimize candidate inputs, combine known attributes with model-derived signals, or use learned inversion models. Useful observations may include prediction scores, probabilities, embeddings, or gradients where exposed.

Results may include inferred sensitive attributes, approximate reconstructions, or representative examples associated with a target identity or class. Such results do not by themselves establish that a reconstructed example was present in the training dataset.

relations.name: Training Data Information from AI Models

objects.name: Extract Memorized Data
objects.description:
Adversaries may elicit and recover sensitive content memorized by a generative AI model during training or fine-tuning. Recovered material may include complete training examples or recognizable portions of text, source code, or images, potentially exposing personal information, private communications, or proprietary material. Recovery may take the form of verbatim reproduction or near-duplicate outputs that reveal specific training content.

Adversaries may supply partial passages, contextual cues, or repeated and varied inputs that encourage reproduction of memorized content. They may generate and filter candidate outputs or compare them with available reference material to identify likely training examples. Researchers have recovered verbatim training passages through language-model queries, including from production systems,[[scalable-extraction]] and extracted memorized training images from diffusion models.[[diffusion-extraction]]

relations.name: Training Data Information from AI Models

objects.name: Indicator Removal
objects.description:
Adversaries may delete, alter, or falsify records and artifacts to conceal their activity, impede investigation, or make unauthorized actions appear legitimate. Targeted artifacts may include logs, command histories, files, metadata, repository history, and published content. Changes may selectively remove suspicious evidence while preserving surrounding material to maintain the appearance of normal activity.

Agents may also conceal activity by modifying artifacts on external collaboration and distribution platforms. Editing public messages, removing malicious content, or rewriting revision history can obscure prior actions, make contributions appear benign, and complicate reconstruction of an attack. These changes may help an agent preserve credibility and continue operating after its activity attracts scrutiny, even when earlier versions remain recoverable.[[aisi]]

Autonomous AI agents may identify and manipulate evidence of their own actions without a human directing each concealment step. Agents may edit or delete accessible transcripts, replace records with misleading content, or tamper with harness components responsible for executing or recording tool calls. Such tampering can cause recorded actions or results to differ from actual execution, undermining oversight that relies on the affected records.[[metr-hf]]

objects.name: Compromise Accounts
objects.description:
Adversaries may compromise existing accounts with services that can support targeting or subsequent operations. These accounts may provide established identities, trusted relationships, access to resources, or funded wallets for AI services.

Adversaries may obtain account credentials through [Phishing](/techniques/AML.T0052), password guessing or reuse, theft of access tokens, or purchase from third parties.

Adversaries may compromise AI service accounts for LLMJacking, a pattern of consuming model access and usage at the account holder's expense.[[sysdig-llmjacking]] Depending on the service, these resources may include prepaid balances or service wallets, promotional credits, subscription allowances, or usage charged to an existing payment method or enterprise billing account. Adversaries may use the acquired capacity for their own inference workloads, code generation, or tool development while exhausting the victim's available credits and quotas or generating additional charges.

Compromised accounts may also supply capacity for [AI Service Proxies](/techniques/AML.T0008.005), allowing operators to aggregate and resell access while concealing the underlying credentials from downstream users.[[sysdig-market]] Google has reported model distillation campaigns that used proxy infrastructure to rotate requests across compromised credentials and fraudulent accounts.[[google-sep]] Account pooling and resale also feature in the gray-market transfer station economy, where account merchants and registration intermediaries supply access alongside discounted capacity, unused quotas, and shared subscriptions.[[chinatalk]].

objects.name: Centralized AI Service Request Routing
objects.description:
Adversaries may distribute coordinated AI service requests across multiple pathways to impede detection, conceal the coordinated nature of the requests, and evade AI provider enforcement. Distributing activity can limit the portion of an operation visible through any individual account or pathway, obscuring its aggregate scale and common objective.

Adversaries may use centralized routing infrastructure to divide a workload or prompt suite across multiple pathways, including various service APIs, cloud-hosted endpoints, third-party aggregators or relays, and account pools. Routers may rotate identities and request pathways, mix adversarial requests with unrelated customer traffic, and automatically redirect requests when requests are blocked. These capabilities allow adversaries to maintain coordinated operations while making the activity appear to originate from unrelated users or services.

Adversaries may also use routing infrastructure to centrally optimize API costs and sustain distributed operations within available quotas and budgets. This may include prioritizing cost-efficient access pathways, allocating quotas across accounts to align with operational budgets, segmenting accounts by purpose, and organizing requests to maximize cache reuse. Centralized routing may coordinate shifts across accounts, providers, or pathways in response to pricing or rate-limit changes, enabling an operation to adapt while continuing to obscure its common control and aggregate activity.

This behavior may be implemented via proxy services (See  [Acquire Infrastructure: AI Service Proxies](/techniques/AML.T0008.005)), multiple cloud instances, IP pools, coordination across multiple accounts, or other distributed infrastructure.

objects.name: AI Service Request Metadata Sanitization
objects.description:
Adversaries may remove or replace identifying information in request metadata before submitting requests to an AI service to impede attribution and correlation of coordinated activity. Sanitization may be enforced automatically in clients, relays, aggregators, or centralized routing infrastructure.

Metadata may include client or device identifiers, session identifiers, account identifiers, client software identifiers, forwarding headers, and attribution markers embedded in request bodies.[[claude-relay-service]] Metadata fields may be sanitized via removal, or replacement with normalized, randomized, or generated values.

The NSA, CISA, and FBI reported removal of organizational identifiers in industrial-scale distillation campaigns, with indicators including the disappearance of previously consistent metadata and generic or randomized patterns replacing organizational markers.[[cisa]]

objects.name: Event Triggered Execution
objects.description:
Adversaries may establish persistence by creating or modifying event handlers, startup hooks, or associated configuration so that subsequent system or application activity automatically executes adversary-controlled code or commands. Triggers may include interpreter initialization, application execution, or other events processed by the affected mechanism. These modifications can allow malicious behavior to recur without another direct execution request from the adversary.

In AI environments, adversaries may target hooks in the software and execution environments used for data processing, model training, evaluation, inference, or agent tool execution. For example, Python startup hooks may execute adversary-controlled code when a subsequent workflow or tool invocation starts an interpreter that processes the hook.[[aisi]] 

Triggered code may perform malicious actions directly or emit content that is subsequently consumed by an AI system. Such content may contain fabricated approvals or instructions intended to manipulate the system's later behavior or make normally unobservable information available. AI Agents may also place triggers or trip-wires behind to observe, act on, or report conditions that the agent can no longer reach or are beyond its execution window.[[metr]]

objects.name: LLM Prompt Propagation
objects.description:
Adversaries may cause malicious instructions already introduced into an AI-enabled environment to be transferred onward to additional storage locations, agents, applications, or resources where they can influence subsequent AI activity. This extends the attack beyond its initial point of introduction and may allow adversaries to influence additional targets without directly delivering a malicious prompt payload to each one.

Propagation may occur through email or other communications, shared documents, source-code repositories, persistent agent memory, retrieval systems, databases, shared workspaces, or direct agent-to-agent communication. Connected tools and services may also carry malicious instructions between otherwise separate environments. The transfer may result from an induced agent action or from copying, forwarding, synchronization, or other workflows that distribute affected content.

objects.name: Recover AI Model Internals
objects.description:
Adversaries may infer or recover non-public AI model internals through analysis of model behavior or exposed information. Targets may include architecture, layer dimensions, hyperparameters, decision-tree structure, projection matrices, or numerical parameters.

Methods may use strategically selected queries, equation solving, numerical reconstruction, or statistical identification. Recovery may be partial, approximate, or exact.

objects.name: Poison AI Agent Learning Environment
objects.description:
Adversaries may manipulate an environment in which an AI agent interacts so that observations, feedback, rewards, actions, or resulting interactions are incorporated into model training to cause persistent changes to the behavior of an AI system. This allows adversary's influence to persist beyond the original interaction and affect subsequent tasks.

An adversary may alter webpages, tool or API responses, elements in simulated environments, task descriptions, reward signals, evaluator outputs, or other environmental content used during AI agent learning or adaptation. The manipulated interactions may be incorporated into model fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, synthetic training corpora, agent memories, other  persistent components.

[Poison AI Agent Learning Environment](/techniques/AML.T0145) targets the process that generates or selects learning experience, without requiring direct adversarial access to training datasets, model parameters, or stored agent artifacts. The resulting experience may appear legitimate because it was produced by an authorized agent operating through an expected interface. Once introduced, the adversary's influence may remain effective even after the manipulated environmental content is removed or is no longer encountered.

An adversary may use this technique to introduce backdoors, increase compliance with malicious instructions, distort policies or preferences, teach unsafe tool use, manipulate reward-seeking behavior. The malicious behavior may be activated later by an environmental trigger or during ordinary agent operation.

objects.name: Limit Public Release of Information
objects.description: Limit the public release of technical information about the AI stack used in an organization's products or services. Technical knowledge of how AI is used can be leveraged by adversaries to perform targeting and tailor attacks to the target system. Additionally, consider limiting the release of organizational information - including physical locations, researcher names, and department structures - from which technical details such as AI techniques, model architectures, or datasets may be inferred.

relations.name: Replicate Behavior from Gathered AI Artifacts
Adapt Existing Model to Replicate Behavior

objects.name: Limit Model Artifact Release
objects.description: Limit public release of technical project details including data, algorithms, model architectures, and model checkpoints that are used in production, or that are representative of those used in production.

relations.name: Replicate Behavior from Gathered AI Artifacts

objects.name: Predictive AI Output Obfuscation
objects.description:
Reduce the fidelity and amount of information returned by predictive AI inference endpoints to make model discovery, extraction, replication, and black-box adversarial-example optimization more difficult.

Limit outputs to those required by the application. Depending on the use case, this may include withholding or reducing the precision of confidence scores, logits, class rankings, labels, embeddings, or additional model metadata.

objects.name: Predictive AI Model Hardening
objects.description:
Design and train predictive AI models to maintain intended performance when presented with adversarial examples. Adversarial examples may include digitally perturbed inputs or physical countermeasures intended to cause misclassification, missed detection, or another attacker-selected prediction.

Robustness techniques may include adversarial training, robust model architectures, defensive distillation, and certified robustness methods.

objects.name: Limit AI Service Query Volume and Rate
objects.description:
Limit the number and rate of requests that users can submit to an AI service. Apply limits by user, API key, tenant, device, or other authenticated identity. Use short-term rate, burst, and concurrency limits together with longer-term usage quotas.

Query limits can increase the time and cost required to extract model information, optimize adversarial inputs, discover system behavior, verify attacks, or overwhelm a service. Monitor for attempts to evade limits through distributed requests, account rotation, or stolen credentials. Query limits may not protect against attacks that require few requests or are performed against an offline model.

relations.name: Spamming AI System with Chaff Data

objects.name: Control Access to AI Models and Data at Rest
objects.description: Establish access controls on internal model registries and limit internal access to production models. Limit access to training data only to approved users.

objects.name: Predictive AI Ensembles
objects.description:
Use an ensemble of diverse predictive AI models to reduce reliance on a single model or model family and improve robustness against adversarial examples.

Ensemble members should be sufficiently diverse, such as through different architectures, training procedures, features, or model families. Combine their predictions using an aggregation or adjudication method designed to prevent an adversarial example that evades one model from controlling the system's predictions.

objects.name: Sanitize Training Data
objects.description:
Detect, quarantine, and remove or remediate poisoned data before it is used to train an AI model. Apply screening when datasets are acquired or updated, and before new data is incorporated into active learning workflows.

Inspect data samples, annotations, and metadata for evidence of manipulation. Depending on the data and intended task, checks may include label inconsistencies, anomalous samples, unexpected shifts in source or class distributions, suspicious duplication or repeated patterns, and backdoor triggers. Compare findings with trusted dataset versions and combine automated screening with targeted review.

Quarantine suspicious records while they are investigated. Remove malicious additions, correct affected labels or annotations, or restore data from a trusted version where appropriate. Repeat screening after remediation and before utilizing the dataset for training tasks.

If affected data has already been used for training, identify the resulting models and evaluate whether retraining, rollback, or other corrective action is needed. Combine sanitization with [Maintain AI Dataset Provenance](/mitigations/AML.M0025) and [Validate AI Model](/mitigations/AML.M0008).

Tools that support screening and sanitizing training data include:

- Adversarial Robustness Toolbox (ART)[[art]]
- Cleanlab[[cleanlab]]

objects.name: Validate AI Model
objects.description:
Evaluate AI models against defined functional requirements before deployment and throughout their operational lifecycle. Validate newly trained or acquired models and repeat evaluation after fine-tuning, model updates, or changes to the conditions in which the model is used.

Use representative evaluation data and adversarial test cases appropriate to the model's capabilities and intended use. Test for unexpected behavior associated with poisoned training data, model tampering, backdoor triggers, adversarial inputs, and sensitive information disclosure. For generative models, include evaluations of susceptibility to prompt injection and jailbreaks, adherence to authorized instructions, and disclosure of information supplied in context or retained through training.

Compare results against trusted baselines or previously evaluated model versions, and investigate significant regressions in performance or unexplained behavior. Use findings to inform model selection, remediation, deployment restrictions, or rollback, and repeat affected evaluations after corrective changes.

During deployment, monitor for changes in model performance and use significant changes to trigger revalidation. Data or concept drift may result from legitimate changes in the operating environment and should be investigated alongside evidence of poisoning or tampering.

objects.name: Predictive AI Multi-Sensor Fusion
objects.description:
Use independent physical sensors (ideally across multiple modalities or from several perspectives) to avoid relying on a single sensor that may be manipulated, obstructed, or disrupted by an adversary.

Relevant sensors may include visible-light cameras, infrared cameras, depth sensors, radar, lidar, microphones, or other physical sensing systems. Corroborate observations across sensors so manipulation of one input source does not overly influence the model's predictions.

objects.name: Predictive AI Input Restoration
objects.description:
Preprocess predictive AI inference inputs to remove, reduce, or disrupt adversarial perturbations before the inputs are evaluated by the model.

Restoration methods may include denoising, compression, reconstruction, resampling, feature squeezing, randomized transformations, or other modality-appropriate preprocessing. Evaluate restoration methods against adaptive adversaries that account for the preprocessing operation.

objects.name: Restrict Library Loading
objects.description:
Prevent abuse of library loading mechanisms in the operating system and software to load untrusted code by configuring appropriate library loading mechanisms and investigating potential vulnerable software.

File formats such as pickle files that are commonly used to store AI models can contain exploits that allow for loading of malicious libraries.

objects.name: Encrypt Sensitive Information
objects.description: Encrypt sensitive data such as AI models to protect against adversaries attempting to access sensitive data.

objects.name: Code Signing
objects.description: Enforce binary and application integrity with digital signature verification to prevent untrusted code from executing. Adversaries can embed malicious code in AI software or models. Developers should also cryptographically sign SBOM and AIBOM components that track model or data provenance. Enforcement of code signing can prevent the compromise of the AI supply chain and prevent execution of malicious code.

objects.name: Verify AI Artifacts
objects.description:
Verify the integrity and authenticity of AI artifacts before importing, loading, or deploying them. Artifacts may include model weights and checkpoints, datasets, tokenizers, model configurations, prompt templates, and agent configuration files. Verify the complete set of files used by the AI system, including supporting files that can alter model or agent behavior.

Compare cryptographic hashes against expected values obtained from an authenticated publisher. Where digital signatures or signed manifests are available, verify that they cover the artifacts being used and were produced by an authorized signer. Do not rely solely on checksums distributed alongside an artifact through the same untrusted or compromised source.

Pin approved artifacts to specific versions and cryptographic digests rather than relying on mutable names, tags, or download locations. Verify artifacts when they are acquired, transferred, or updated, and before they are loaded or interpreted.

Successful verification establishes that an artifact matches a trusted reference or was signed by an accepted identity. It does not establish that the artifact is free of malicious code, poisoned data, backdoors, or harmful instructions. Combine artifact verification with [Vulnerability Scanning](/mitigations/AML.M0016) and [Validate AI Model](/mitigations/AML.M0008).

objects.name: Predictive AI Adversarial Input Detection
objects.description:
Detect and block digital or physical adversarial examples submitted to predictive AI models. Adversarial examples are inputs modified or constructed to cause misclassification, missed detection, excessive computation, or another attacker-selected behavior.

Apply detection before model inference and monitor for input characteristics or query patterns associated with adversarial example generation, transfer attacks, or black-box optimization. Detection may use statistical tests, auxiliary models, consistency checks, input distribution analysis, or modality-specific adversarial example detectors.

objects.name: Vulnerability Scanning
objects.description:
Vulnerability scanning is used to find potentially exploitable software vulnerabilities to remediate them.

File formats such as pickle files that are commonly used to store AI models can contain exploits that allow for arbitrary code execution.
These files should be scanned for potentially unsafe calls, which could be used to execute code, create new processes, or establish networking capabilities.
Adversaries may embed malicious code in corrupt model files, so scanners should be capable of working with models that cannot be fully de-serialized.
Model artifacts, downstream products produced by models, and external software dependencies should be scanned for known vulnerabilities.

objects.name: AI Model Distribution Methods
objects.description:
Deploying AI models to edge devices can increase the attack surface of the system.
Consider serving models in the cloud to reduce the level of access the adversary has to the model.
Also consider computing features in the cloud to prevent gray-box attacks, where an adversary has access to the model preprocessing methods.

objects.name: User Training
objects.description:
Educate AI model developers to on AI supply chain risks and potentially malicious AI artifacts.
Educate users on how to identify deepfakes and phishing attempts.

objects.name: Control Access to AI Models and Data in Production
objects.description:
Require users to verify their identities before accessing a production model.
Require authentication for API endpoints and monitor production model queries to ensure compliance with usage policies and to prevent model misuse.

relations.name: Spamming AI System with Chaff Data

objects.name: Generative AI Guardrails
objects.description:
Guardrails are safety controls placed between users, tools, and generative AI models to evaluate prompts, retrieved context, model outputs, and agent actions before they are accepted, executed, or shown to a user. They can help block, modify, or route unwanted content such as malicious code, malicious instructions, sensitive data, unsupported claims, policy-violating responses, or unsafe tool requests.

Guardrails can be implemented using rule-based controls such as filters, allowlists, blocklists, regular expressions, schema validation, policy rules, and permission checks, or using AI-based techniques such as classifiers, LLM reviewers/judges, named entity recognition, groundedness checks, and task-adherence checks. They may be applied at multiple stages of a generative AI workflow, including input handling, prompt construction, retrieval, tool execution, model output review, and post-deployment monitoring.

Examples of specific guardrail implementations include:[[owasp-llm-top10]]  [[datadog-llm-guardrails]] [[azure-ai-content-safety]] [[nvidia-nemo-guardrails]]
- Input moderation: Screen user prompts for harmful content, prompt injection attempts, jailbreak attempts, sensitive data, off-topic requests, or inputs that exceed expected length or format.
- Output moderation: Scan model responses before sending them to users for harmful content, PII, secrets, policy violations, unsupported claims, or unsafe code using classical scanners, classifiers, or a dedicated reviewer model .
- System prompt and policy enforcement: Enforce system instructions, user roles, domain boundaries, response formats, and refusal policies before the model responds (See [Generative AI Guidelines](/mitigations/AML.M0021)).
- Tool and action guardrails: Validate tool calls, tool arguments, permissions, and tool outputs before execution or before results are returned to the model. Require human approval for high-impact, irreversible, privileged, or externally visible actions (See [Human In-the-Loop for AI Agent Actions](/mitigations/AML.M0029), [Input and Output Validation for AI Agent Components](/mitigations/AML.M0033)).
- Retrieval guardrails: Filter and validate retrieved documents before they are added to model context, including checks for untrusted sources, malicious instructions, irrelevant context, or sensitive data.
- Groundedness and factuality checks: Compare model responses against trusted source material or approved knowledge bases to detect unsupported or hallucinated claims.
- Sensitive data and secret protection: Detect, redact, or block personal information, credentials, tokens, proprietary data, system prompts, and other confidential information in prompts, retrieved context, tool outputs, and model responses.
- Structured output validation: Enforce schemas, type checks, allowed values, and safe formats before model outputs are consumed by downstream systems

Guardrails should be continuously evaluated, red-teamed, and updated as adversarial techniques evolve. Guardrail decisions should be logged (See [AI Telemetry Logging and Monitoring](/mitigations/AML.M0024)) and observed failures should be systematically incorporated into updated policies, evaluation datasets, detection logic, prompts, and [Generative AI Model Alignment](/mitigations/AML.M0022).

objects.name: Generative AI Guidelines
objects.description:
Guidelines are instructions, policies, and behavioral constraints provided to a generative AI model to direct it toward desired outputs and away from unsafe, unreliable, or policy-violating behavior. Guidelines can help reduce risks related to organization policy violations, brand damage, private data leakage, false or unsupported information, unsafe advice, and misuse of tools or external content.

Guidelines can be implemented as system prompts, prompt templates, policy text appended to user prompts, or task-specific instructions included during prompt construction. They can define the system's goals, role, tone, allowed and disallowed behavior, domain boundaries, citation requirements, data-handling expectations, escalation criteria, and safety or security rules.

Common prompt elements include:
- Instructions to cite sources or identify when an answer is not supported by available context.
- Instructions to treat external, retrieved, or user-provided content as untrusted data rather than authoritative sources.
- Instructions to avoid revealing system prompts, hidden policies, credentials, private data, or other sensitive information.
- Instructions to stay within the application's approved domain and refuse requests outside that scope.
- Instructions to follow organization-specific policies, brand requirements, and regulated-domain restrictions.
- Instructions to request human approval before proceeding with potentially unsafe, privileged, irreversible, or externally visible actions when untrusted content is in context (See [Human In-the-Loop for AI Agent Actions](/mitigations/AML.M0029)).

Guidelines should be tested, red-teamed, and updated as observed failures, prompt injection techniques, policy requirements, and application capabilities evolve. Guidelines are most effective when paired with [Generative AI Guardrails](/mitigations/AML.M0020) that validate inputs, outputs, retrieved context, and tool use.

objects.name: Generative AI Model Alignment
objects.description:
Generative AI Model Alignment is the process of training or fine-tuning a generative model to guide its output toward a set of human values, goals, or ethical principles. Desired principles can be in alignment with safety, security, content policies, and legal requirements, with goals such as removing harmful content or hallucinations, reducing biases, increasing predictability, and ensuring models do not have adverse societal consequences. In the context of agentic AI, alignment is about producing models that make decisions in support of the goals of the organization and individual users, with actions that remain in scope of the designated task, and designing agents that follow security standards, exhibit transparency in decision making, and operate within organizational boundaries.

Common methods for aligning a generative model during training or fine-tuning include[[ibm-llm-alignment]][[meta-llama]]:
- Reinforcement Learning from Human or AI Feedback (RLHF or RLAIF)
- Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT)
- Targeted Safety Context Distillation
- Instruction Tuning
- Direct Preference Optimization (DPO)
- Constitutional AI
- Incoulation Prompting

For agentic systems, alignment depends on the purpose of the agent, the tools available to the agent, and the levels of privileges and risks associated with tool calls. Standard alignment methods for LLMs can often be used in conjunction with domain-specific fine-tuning data, reward signals with examples of correct tool calls, or reinforcement learning based on interactions with a realistic environment. Examples of alignment methods specific to agentic AI are:
- Trajectory Preference Optimization[[tpmm-dpo]]
- Environment-Driven Reinforcement Learning[[envrl]]
- Reinforcement Learning with Execution Feedback (RLEF)[[rlef]]
- Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR)[[nvidia-mastering-agentic]]

Generative AI Model Alignment should be used in combination with [Generative AI Guardrails](/mitigations/AML.M0020) and [Generative AI Guidelines](/mitigations/AML.M0021). Models should be continually evaluated for alignment and retrained or fine-tuned systematically to incorporate observed failure modes or updated policies. It is important to also consider that fine-tuning a model can remove previously learned alignments and should be undertaken with care and a comprehensive plan for testing the updated model for safety and security.

objects.name: Maintain an AI Bill of Materials
objects.description:
Create and maintain an AI Bill of Materials (AI BOM) that identifies the components and dependencies used to build, evaluate, and operate an AI-enabled system. Include models and checkpoints, datasets, software packages, inference runtimes, container images, and agent configurations including system instructions and connected tools and data sources. For systems that use external AI services or agent tools, record the relevant providers, services, integrations, and available version identifiers.

Record component identifiers, versions, sources, suppliers or publishers, and cryptographic digests. Capture dependency and derivation relationships, such as which base model and dataset versions produced a fine-tuned model. Link to supporting provenance, integrity-verification, and evaluation records rather than treating inclusion in the AI BOM as evidence of approval or safety.

Generate or update the AI BOM when components are acquired, built, modified, or deployed. Retain version history and protect records from unauthorized modification. Identify gaps where upstream information or hosted-service version details are unavailable.

Use the AI BOM to assess component changes, correlate security advisories and reports of compromised artifacts with deployed systems, and trace affected dependencies and derived models. Use these findings to prioritize investigation, replacement, rollback, or retraining.

An AI BOM provides inventory and traceability. It does not establish that a listed component is authentic, unmodified, or free of malicious behavior. Combine it with [Verify AI Artifacts](/mitigations/AML.M0014), [Maintain AI Dataset Provenance](/mitigations/AML.M0025), and [Validate AI Model](/mitigations/AML.M0008).

objects.name: AI Telemetry Logging and Monitoring
objects.description:
Implement logging and monitoring across the AI lifecycle to detect suspicious activity and support investigation. Capture security-relevant access, changes, and operations across data pipelines, model development, deployment, and connected systems. Preserve sufficient context to trace activity across components and identify coordinated behavior across accounts and access pathways.

Tailor telemetry to each system's function, including relevant data and model versions, request and execution metadata, and operation results. For agentic systems, distinguish requested actions from those actually executed, using independent service records where available. Treat model-generated explanations and summaries as supporting context rather than authoritative evidence of execution.

Monitor individual events and patterns over time for anomalous access, unauthorized changes, unusual usage, and unexpected model behavior or external actions. Correlate findings with related operational activity to guide investigation and response.

Protect telemetry from unauthorized access, modification, or deletion, and monitor for gaps in coverage. Limit the collection of sensitive content through metadata, references, or redaction where these preserve investigative value, and apply appropriate retention controls.

objects.name: Maintain AI Dataset Provenance
objects.description: Maintain a detailed history of datasets used for AI applications. The history should include information about the dataset's source as well as a complete record of any modifications.

objects.name: Manage AI Agent Service Access
objects.description:
Limit service AI agents--agents using independently assigned service or workload permissions--to explicitly authorized workflows. Agents may serve multiple users or act on requests, events, or schedules. Examples include service desk agents fulfilling support requests, operations agents restarting services after monitoring alerts, and reporting agents reading organizational data and publishing scheduled summaries. Apply least privilege to identities, roles, credentials, tools, and resources; permission to invoke an agent must not confer all its authority.

Controls should include:

- Dedicated Agent Identity: Use identifiable service or workload identities scoped to agent functions. Avoid unrestricted administrator accounts and broadly privileged identities shared across unrelated workflows.
- Scoped Roles and Permissions: Use role-based or attribute-based controls to limit workflows to required operations and resources. Separate routine access from permission changes, credential management, security configuration, and deletion.
- Workflow Initiation Authorization: Use trusted identity and authorization context to verify that requesters or triggers may initiate the specific workflow and affect its target resources.
- Privilege Separation: Separate materially different workflows through distinct roles, credentials, or execution contexts. Prevent cross-workflow reuse of credentials or authorization state without explicit authorization.
- Service Access Lifecycle Management: Limit elevated-access duration where supported, review grants as responsibilities change, and revoke unnecessary credentials or roles. Prevent unauthorized users and the agent itself from modifying permission configurations.

An agent may perform operations unavailable directly to its requester, such as fulfilling an approved administrative request, but the requester must be authorized to initiate that workflow. Limit execution authority to the operations and resources needed to fulfill it.

Use [Enforce Access Controls for AI Agent Tools](/mitigations/AML.M0028) to enforce these restrictions when tools execute requests, and [AI Agent Authority Expansion Controls](/mitigations/AML.M0037) to govern attempts to obtain additional authority during execution. Record the initiating user, application, service, event, or schedule, agent execution identity, authorization decision, and resulting activity through [AI Telemetry Logging and Monitoring](/mitigations/AML.M0024).

Tools that may help implement these controls include:

- Microsoft Entra ID: Provides service principals, managed identities, and application permissions for workloads. Workload identity federation supports authentication without stored application secrets where supported; Entra Agent ID provides agent-specific identities with directly assigned access.[[entra-workload-identities]][[entra-agent-identities]]
- Amazon Web Services IAM: Provides workload roles and temporary credentials scoped to required actions, resources, and conditions. IAM Access Analyzer supports permission review, policy validation, and policy generation from observed access.[[aws-iam-best-practices]]

objects.name: Manage User-Delegated AI Agent Access
objects.description:
Limit user-delegated AI agents to explicitly authorized tasks and permissions. Apply the principle of least privilege so that the agent receives only the access required for its designated tasks. The user's permissions establish an upper bound; the agent should not automatically receive every permission available to that user.

Controls should include:

- Agent Identity and User Association: Bind an identifiable agent or application identity to the authorizing user. Distinguish both identities in access decisions and activity records.
- Scoped Delegation: Limit operations, resources, and services to the required subset of user permissions, using read-only access where sufficient. Derive scope from trusted configuration or authorization mechanisms, not the agent's interpretation of requests.
- Credential and Session Management: Use scoped, short-lived credentials where supported. Keep credentials outside model-visible context, isolate them across users' agents and sessions, and avoid broadly privileged shared accounts.
- Access Lifecycle Management: Review delegation when tasks or user permissions change, and reflect removed user permissions in effective agent access. Expire or revoke credentials and sessions when delegation ends, the agent is decommissioned, or compromise is suspected.

Enforce delegated permissions through the systems that provide access to tools and resources. Use [Enforce Access Controls for AI Agent Tools](/mitigations/AML.M0028) to ensure that tool calls remain within the user's delegation, including when tools invoke downstream services. Use [AI Agent Authority Expansion Controls](/mitigations/AML.M0037) to prevent the agent from autonomously obtaining additional authority outside its approved scope.

Tools that may help implement these controls include:

- Microsoft Entra ID: Supports user-delegated permissions, user and administrator consent, and token acquisition on behalf of users. Entra Agent ID provides agent-specific identities with delegated access bounded by granted permissions and the user's authorized access.[[entra-permissions-consent]][[entra-agent-identities]]
- Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity: Provides agent workload identities and centralized credential management for AWS and third-party services. User-authorized OAuth integrations support access on behalf of users.[[agentcode-identity]]

objects.name: Enforce Access Controls for AI Agent Tools
objects.description:
Limit AI agent tool access to each caller's authorized, task-required operations and resources, including when tools are shared across agents, users, or tenants. Broader tool or backend privileges must not expand caller access. Enforce controls outside the model, in the tool implementation, MCP server, gateway, or underlying service.

Enforce access controls outside the model: in the tool implementation, MCP server, access gateway, or underlying service. Controls should include:

- Caller Authentication: Authenticate calling agents and derive identity, tenant, and delegation context from trusted authentication mechanisms, not model-generated arguments.
- Request Authorization: Authorize each action on its target resource, separately controlling read, modify, and delete permissions. Deny requests when authorization cannot be established.
- Delegated Access Enforcement: Enforce delegated permissions, trusted task restrictions, and tool policy through downstream calls. Use credentials scoped to each receiving service without expanding caller access.
- Access Isolation: Isolate users' credentials, sessions, and authorization context. Select downstream credentials using verified caller context and prevent shared tool state from exposing another caller's resources.

Tools that may help implement these controls include:

- Open Policy Agent (OPA): Evaluates tool requests against caller identity, operations, resources, and trusted context. Tool services or gateways enforce the resulting least-privilege and caller-specific access decisions.[[opa]]
- Cedar: Provides an authorization policy language and engine for evaluating caller actions on resources in context. Supports role- and attribute-based restrictions on tool operations and resources.[[cedar]]

objects.name: Human In-the-Loop for AI Agent Actions
objects.description:
Systems should require the user or another human stakeholder to approve AI agent actions before the agent takes them. The human approver may be technical staff or business unit SMEs depending on the use case. Separate tools, such as dedicated audit agents, may assist human approval, but final adjudication should be conducted by a human decision-maker. 

The security benefits from Human In-the-Loop policies may be at odds with operational overhead costs of additional approvals. To ease this, Human In-the-Loop policies should follow the degree of consequence of the task at hand. Minor, repetitive tasks performed by agents accessing basic tools may only require minimal human oversight, while agents employed in systems with significant consequences may necessitate approval from multiple stakeholders diversified across multiple organizations.

objects.name: Restrict AI Agent Tool Invocation on Untrusted Data
objects.description:
Untrusted data can contain prompt injections that invoke an AI agent's tools, potentially causing confidentiality, integrity or availability violations. It is recommended that tool invocation be restricted or limited when untrusted data enters the LLM's context.

The degree to which tool invocation is restricted may depend on the potential consequences of the action. Consider blocking the automatic invocation of tools or requiring user confirmation once untrusted data enters the LLM's context. For high consequence actions, consider always requiring user confirmation.
